title: Quality Assurance & Coding Standards
subtitle: Lecture-based guide: SQA, faults and failures, reliability metrics, testing, reviews, and enforceable coding standards.
contentMarkdown:
## Scope and source

Based on the supplied **L29 - Software Quality Assurance.md**, assigned to **L30** by the updated scope. This rewrite keeps the lecture ideas, but explains them in a slower study style with more examples and reasons.

## 1. What does “quality” mean in software?

Software quality means more than “the program runs.” A system can run and still be poor quality if it is insecure, confusing, unreliable, hard to change, or too slow.

The notes describe quality as meeting:

1. explicit functional and performance requirements
2. documented development standards
3. implicit professional expectations

The third one is important. A specification may forget to say “do not leak student marks to other students,” but users and professionals still expect confidentiality. So quality is not only about blindly matching a written document. It is also about reasonable expectations for the kind of system being built.

Examples of quality attributes:

| Attribute | Simple meaning |
|---|---|
| Reliability | Works without failing for a period of use |
| Availability | Is up and usable when needed |
| Security | Protects data and actions from unauthorised use |
| Usability | Real users can complete tasks without unnecessary confusion |
| Maintainability | Developers can understand and change it safely |
| Testability | Behaviour can be checked with reasonable effort |
| Portability | Can move across environments where required |
| Efficiency | Uses resources responsibly |

Quality attributes can conflict. Extra security checks can add complexity. More replicas can improve availability but increase cost. Highly optimised code can become harder to understand. A good answer explains the trade-off in context.

## 2. SQA versus quality control

This distinction is central:

| Term | Easy meaning | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Software Quality Assurance (SQA) | Setting up and checking the process that should produce quality | Process |
| Quality Control (QC) | Checking the actual product/artifact for defects | Product |

SQA asks: “Do we have the right practices, standards, reviews, tests, and controls?”

QC asks: “Does this requirement, design, code, or test result contain a problem?”

Testing is quality control, but quality work is bigger than testing. Reviews, coding standards, change control, measurements, and defect tracking all contribute.

The lecture's three-part approach:

1. Establish organisation-wide policies and standards.
2. Tailor procedures and standards for the project.
3. Check that the agreed process is actually followed.

Why step 3 matters: a standards document that nobody uses does not improve quality. Evidence matters. Examples include review records, CI results, test reports, defect logs, and approved exceptions.

## 3. Why quality assurance is worth doing

SQA costs time and effort. Reviews take time. Tests take time. Standards can feel restrictive. Tooling must be configured. People must learn the process.

But skipping assurance often moves the cost later, where it is more expensive. A requirements ambiguity caught in a review may take minutes to clarify. The same ambiguity found after deployment may require emergency fixes, data repair, user communication, and lost trust.

Benefits include:

- fewer hidden defects
- less rework
- easier maintenance
- better reliability
- clearer team expectations
- stronger evidence for assessment or release decisions

The goal is not maximum paperwork. The goal is assurance effort that matches the risk. A safety-critical feature deserves stronger assurance than a temporary internal prototype.

## 4. Faults and failures

A **fault** is the defect in the artifact. A **failure** is the incorrect behaviour you observe when the system runs.

Example:

```text
Fault: The leap-year condition in code is wrong.
Failure: A valid 29 February booking is rejected.
```

The fault can exist for months without a visible failure if nobody uses the affected date. This is why “we have not seen a failure” does not prove “there are no faults.”

The lecture categories help you explain where defects come from:

| Code | Cause | Plain explanation |
|---|---|---|
| IES | Incomplete or erroneous specifications | The requirement was missing or wrong |
| MCC | Misinterpreted customer communication | The team misunderstood the stakeholder |
| IDS | Intentional deviation from specifications | Someone knowingly built something different |
| EDL | Error in design logic | The design reasoning was wrong |
| EDR | Error in data representation | Data was modelled or stored incorrectly |
| PLT | Error translating design into code | The implementation did not match the design |
| ICI | Inconsistent component interfaces | Components do not agree on contract or format |
| VPS | Violation of programming standards | Code breaks agreed rules |
| IET | Incomplete or erroneous testing | Tests miss important cases or assert the wrong thing |
| IID | Inaccurate or incomplete documentation | Docs mislead developers or users |
| HCI | Ambiguous or inconsistent human/computer interface | UI causes confusion or wrong use |

The bigger picture: not every defect is “a bad line of code.” Some defects start in requirements, communication, design, interfaces, or tests.

## 5. Reliability and availability

Reliability and availability are related, but different.

**Reliability** asks: how long can the system operate without failure under stated conditions?

**Availability** asks: when users need it, is it operational?

A system can fail often but recover quickly. That may give decent availability but poor reliability. Users still experience interruptions. A system can also fail rarely but take a long time to restore, damaging availability.

Lecture formulas:

```text
MTTF = total observed operating time / number of failures
MTTR = total observed repair time / number of repairs
MTBF = MTTF + MTTR
Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) x 100%
```

Meanings:

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| MTTF | Average time the system runs before a failure |
| MTTR | Average time to repair or restore |
| MTBF | Average full cycle from one failure to the next under the lecture convention |
| Availability | Proportion of time expected to be operational |

Worked example:

```text
Operating times: 180 + 220 + 200 = 600 hours
Failures: 3
Repair times: 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 hours
Repairs: 3

MTTF = 600 / 3 = 200 h
MTTR = 12 / 3 = 4 h
MTBF = 200 + 4 = 204 h
Availability = 200 / 204 x 100 = 98.04%
```

If MTTR improves from 4 hours to 1 hour, availability becomes:

```text
200 / 201 x 100 = 99.50%
```

Notice the “why”: faster repair can improve availability even if the underlying fault still exists. Reliability and recovery should be discussed separately.

## 6. Metrics: useful indicators, not magic proof

A metric is a measurement of a product, process, or artifact. Metrics help you reason, but they do not automatically prove quality.

| Metric type | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Control metric | Helps manage the process | Effort spent, elapsed time, defect count |
| Predictor metric | Estimates another quality | Complexity as an indicator of maintainability risk |
| Internal attribute | Measured from the product itself | Lines of code, fan-out |
| External attribute | Observed through use | Failure rate, time to complete task |

Maintainability depends on things like cohesion, coupling, understandability, and adaptability. A number can point to a risk, but context still matters.

**Fan-in** counts how many other components call or depend on a component. High fan-in may mean useful reuse, but also high change impact.

**Fan-out** counts how many components this component calls or depends on. High fan-out can make testing and reasoning harder because more collaborators are involved.

Information-flow complexity in the notes:

```text
component length x (fan-in x fan-out)^2
```

For length 10, fan-in 2, fan-out 3:

```text
10 x (2 x 3)^2
= 10 x 6^2
= 10 x 36
= 360
```

This is not cyclomatic complexity. Cyclomatic complexity is about independent control-flow paths through code.

## 7. Choosing the right quality check

Different tests answer different questions:

| Check | Main question |
|---|---|
| Unit test | Does this small unit behave correctly with dependencies controlled? |
| Integration test | Do real parts work together across a boundary? |
| Regression test | Did a change break something that used to work? |
| Non-functional test | Does the system meet qualities like performance or resilience? |
| Acceptance test | Does it meet user/stakeholder acceptance conditions? |
| Configuration test | Does it work across supported settings/environments? |
| Adapter/interface test | Does it correctly speak to an external protocol or UI boundary? |

Mocking is useful in unit tests because it isolates the unit. But if you mock the exact boundary you claim to be integrating, you have not proven that real integration works.

Example: a mocked database adapter can prove the caller handles a returned value. It cannot prove the real database query, credentials, schema, network, and serialization work.

Testing techniques:

| Technique | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Equivalence partitioning | Choose representatives from groups expected to behave similarly | One valid age, one invalid negative age |
| Boundary value analysis | Test edges where mistakes often occur | 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101 for range 1-100 |
| Path analysis | Use code structure to test control-flow paths | White-box tests for branches |

## 8. Coding standards that actually help

Coding standards should make code easier to read, review, test, and maintain. They should not be empty rules followed only for appearance.

A useful standard includes:

- meaningful names
- consistent formatting
- clear responsibilities
- exception-handling rules
- input validation expectations
- security hygiene
- commenting guidance
- test expectations
- version-control conventions

The important part is the reason behind the rule.

Example:

```python
# Bad: hides every error and reports success.
def charge(order):
    try:
        gateway.charge(order)
    except Exception:
        return True
```

Why this is dangerous: if the payment gateway timed out after possibly charging the customer, returning `True` lies to the rest of the system. The system may mark the order as paid without knowing the real payment state.

Better idea:

```python
def charge(order):
    try:
        return gateway.charge(order)
    except GatewayTimeout as error:
        raise PaymentStatusUnknown(order.id) from error
```

Now the code communicates the uncertainty. The business process can reconcile the payment or retry safely using an idempotency rule.

Tools help enforce standards:

| Tool/check | What it does |
|---|---|
| Formatter | Applies layout consistently |
| Linter/static analyser | Checks configured rules and possible defects |
| Tests | Check expected behaviour |
| CI | Runs checks consistently for submitted changes |
| Human review | Checks meaning, design, trade-offs, and context |

Local hooks are useful, but they can be bypassed. CI gives a shared gate.

## Exam answer pattern

For quality questions:

1. Define the term.
2. Distinguish it from a nearby term.
3. Apply it to the scenario.
4. State what evidence would support the claim.

Example: “SQA is process-focused, while QC is product-focused. In this project, requiring code reviews and CI checks is SQA; finding a failing boundary test is QC evidence. The claim is supported by review records, test results, and defect follow-up.”
tldr: Quality includes **explicit requirements, standards and implicit expectations**.
**SQA governs processes; QC checks products**. Reviews and testing both contribute.
A **fault** is a defect; a **failure** is observed incorrect runtime behaviour.
Lecture formulas: **MTBF = MTTF + MTTR**, availability = MTTF / MTBF.
Metrics are **indicators**, not automatic proof of maintainability or correctness.
Know unit, integration, regression, acceptance, configuration and adapter testing.
Coding standards need **purpose, examples, automation and demonstrated compliance**.

mcqs.q: Why is conformance to a specification alone insufficient for quality?
options: The specification may omit implicit expectations or be ambiguous
mcqs.explanation: The notes include explicit requirements, development standards and implicit professional expectations.

mcqs.q: Which activity is primarily process-oriented SQA?
options: Establishing and checking project review procedures
mcqs.explanation: SQA concerns the practices used to produce and sustain quality.

mcqs.q: What is a software fault?
options: A static defect that can cause a failure
mcqs.explanation: A fault may remain dormant until particular inputs or states activate it.

mcqs.q: What is a software failure?
options: An unexecuted defective branch by itself
Observed incorrect or unexpected runtime behaviour
mcqs.explanation: Failure refers to behaviour, while a fault is the underlying defect.

mcqs.q: Which defect category covers mismatched component interfaces?
mcqs.explanation: The notes use ICI for inconsistent component interfaces.

mcqs.q: Uptimes are 180, 220 and 200 hours. What is MTTF for these cycles?
mcqs.explanation: Divide the 600 observed operating hours by three failures.

mcqs.q: Repair times are 3, 5 and 4 hours. What is MTTR?
mcqs.explanation: The mean repair duration is 12 divided by three.

mcqs.q: Under the lecture convention, MTTF is 200 h and MTTR is 4 h. What is MTBF?
mcqs.explanation: The notes define MTBF as MTTF plus MTTR.

mcqs.q: What availability follows from MTTF 200 h and MTTR 4 h?
mcqs.explanation: Availability is 200 divided by 204, multiplied by 100 percent.

mcqs.q: What can improve availability without increasing MTTF?
mcqs.explanation: Faster recovery reduces the proportion of time unavailable.

mcqs.q: Which is a predictor metric example?
options: The number of days in a semester
Complexity used as an indicator of maintenance difficulty
mcqs.explanation: Predictor metrics link a measurable attribute to another product quality.

mcqs.q: What does structural fan-out measure?
options: Outgoing calls or dependencies from a component under a defined counting rule
The time to restore a backup
mcqs.explanation: Fan-out concerns how many other components the component depends on.

mcqs.q: Length is 10, informational fan-in is 2 and fan-out is 3. What is the lecture's information-flow complexity?
mcqs.explanation: Apply length × (fan-in × fan-out)²: 10 × 36 = 360.

mcqs.q: Which test needs real collaboration across the boundary being evaluated?
options: A mocked unit test of one function
mcqs.explanation: Replacing that boundary with a mock prevents verifying its real integration behaviour.

mcqs.q: What is regression testing?
options: Checking that changes have not broken previously supported behaviour or qualities
mcqs.explanation: Regression checks may include functional and non-functional tests.

mcqs.q: Which method chooses values immediately around limits?
mcqs.explanation: Boundary checks target likely off-by-one and limit-handling defects.

mcqs.q: Which method is white-box?
mcqs.explanation: Path analysis uses internal control flow to identify test paths.

mcqs.q: Why are local pre-commit hooks insufficient by themselves?
options: They can be bypassed and need consistent CI enforcement
mcqs.explanation: Shared CI checks provide a consistent gate for submitted changes.

mcqs.q: What is wrong with catching every exception and returning success?
options: It makes the code strongly typed
It hides failures and can violate business correctness
mcqs.explanation: Recovery must be deliberate; reporting success after an unknown failure can corrupt workflow state.

mcqs.q: Which comment provides the most useful rationale?
options: Assert the code can never fail
Explain why a retry must use the same payment identifier
Repeat that x is assigned to x
Copy the next line word for word
mcqs.explanation: Comments should clarify intent and non-obvious constraints rather than duplicate obvious syntax.

techQuestions.q: Explain the three-part SQA approach and apply it to a student project.
techQuestions.answer: Start with organisation-level templates for review, tests and change control. Tailor them to the project's language, risks and team size, then verify that the team follows them through CI evidence, review records and spot checks. A template alone is insufficient. Assign an owner and periodically review whether the practices catch meaningful defects without unnecessary overhead.

techQuestions.q: Why can software meet written requirements and still have poor quality?
techQuestions.answer: Requirements may omit expected security, usability or recovery behaviour, or describe it ambiguously. A feature-complete results portal that exposes another student's records violates an implicit quality expectation. Clarify such expectations into measurable acceptance criteria. Consider competing attributes and document trade-offs instead of assuming every quality can be maximised simultaneously.

techQuestions.q: Distinguish a fault and a failure with an example and a testing implication.
techQuestions.answer: An incorrect date condition in source code is a fault. Rejecting a valid leap-day booking when that branch runs is a failure. If tests never use the affected date, the fault can remain unobserved. Choose partitions and boundaries likely to exercise dormant defects; do not conclude that a passing test suite proves the implementation fault-free.

techQuestions.q: Calculate all reliability metrics from the lecture's three observed cycles.
techQuestions.answer: Operating times total 600 hours and repairs total 12 hours. MTTF = 600/3 = 200 h; MTTR = 12/3 = 4 h. Using the lecture convention, MTBF = 204 h and availability = 200/204 × 100 = 98.04%. State the observation scope and units; these sample averages are estimates, not guarantees for an entire future semester.

techQuestions.q: Compare reducing faults with improving restoration procedures.
techQuestions.answer: Removing a recurrent fault may increase the time between failures, supporting reliability. Automated recovery or clearer runbooks may reduce repair time, increasing availability even if failure frequency remains unchanged. Measure both effects separately. With MTTF 200 h, reducing MTTR from 4 h to 1 h raises the availability estimate from 98.04% to 99.50% without changing MTTF.

techQuestions.q: How should a team interpret a component with high fan-in?
techQuestions.answer: Many callers suggest reuse and potential wide impact if the component changes. The lecture associates this with coupling, but it is not automatically a reason to duplicate a useful shared service. Inspect interface stability, caller assumptions and test coverage. Use the metric to prioritise review and compatibility checks rather than treating a high number as proof of bad design.

techQuestions.q: Compare control metrics, predictor metrics and external quality attributes.
techQuestions.answer: Effort and elapsed time help manage the development process and are control metrics. Code complexity is directly measurable and can be used as a predictor of maintenance difficulty. Ease of maintenance is assessed through actual work and depends on context. Validate the relationship with project evidence; optimising a predictor alone can fail to improve the quality users or maintainers experience.

techQuestions.q: Design tests for an integer input accepted only from 1 to 100.
techQuestions.answer: Partition into valid integers, integers below the minimum, integers above the maximum and invalid types or formats as appropriate to the interface. Test representative values and boundaries 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101. Assert the intended result or error. If internal branching matters, supplement these black-box cases with path-based checks rather than assuming boundaries cover every branch.

techQuestions.q: How do unit, integration and regression testing complement each other?
techQuestions.answer: Unit tests isolate a responsibility and check outputs or postconditions. Integration tests exercise real interactions, such as API serialization and database behaviour. Regression testing is a purpose applied after change across these levels and relevant non-functional checks. Mocks help isolation but cannot establish that the substituted real integration works. Select checks based on the changed behaviour and dependencies.

techQuestions.q: Draft a practical coding-standard policy outline.
techQuestions.answer: State goals such as readability, safe failure handling and consistent collaboration. Define naming and formatting, responsibility boundaries, exception rules, documentation, testing, security hygiene and commit conventions. Include good and bad code examples, tool configuration and how CI enforces it. Explain exceptions and review responsibility. Demonstrate compliance in actual code rather than only listing tool names in a report.

techQuestions.q: Review the payment function that catches every exception and returns true.
techQuestions.answer: It converts unknown outcomes into apparent success and hides errors from monitoring and callers. Handle specific expected failures, preserve useful context and expose an accurate domain outcome such as payment status unknown. Verify provider status or retry with a stable idempotency mechanism. Test successful payment, timeout and explicit rejection; an exception policy must preserve business correctness.

techQuestions.q: How can a small team adopt SQA without excessive ceremony?
techQuestions.answer: Choose lightweight practices tied to its highest risks: a short requirements review, automated formatting and tests, peer review of sensitive changes, and a defect log with owners. Reuse templates and measure whether rework or escaped defects improve. Budget time for setup and maintenance. Expand controls where evidence warrants it rather than copying every process from a much larger organisation.

learning.title: Trace one defect through assurance and control
learning.intro: This is an example lifecycle, not a promise that every defect follows one path. Select the stage to see what evidence it contributes.

steps.label: Agree rules
steps.title: 1. Prevent ambiguity
steps.explanation: Quality starts with explicit requirements and expected qualities. A shared error-handling standard gives reviewers something concrete to evaluate.
steps.example: The payment workflow must never report confirmed success for an unknown outcome.
steps.trap: A standards document with no examples or enforcement is weak assurance.

steps.label: Review change
steps.title: 2. Inspect the artifact
steps.explanation: Review requirements, design and code for contradictions and unsafe assumptions. A static fault can be found before anyone observes a runtime failure.
steps.example: A reviewer notices catch-all handling that returns success after a payment timeout.
steps.trap: Passing formatting checks does not establish correct business semantics.

steps.label: Exercise behaviour
steps.title: 3. Activate the important paths
steps.explanation: Test positive, negative and boundary cases with meaningful assertions. Use real collaborators when claiming evidence about an integration.
steps.example: Force a timeout after a provider may have accepted payment; assert an unknown state rather than paid.
steps.trap: No exception was thrown is not a sufficient assertion for every service.

steps.label: Learn from operation
steps.title: 4. Measure and improve
steps.explanation: Observe incidents and repair duration, then feed defects back into requirements, standards and regression coverage. Interpret metrics with their units and context.
steps.example: A runbook shortens restoration time even before the underlying fault is removed.
steps.trap: Better availability does not necessarily mean fewer failures.

learning.labIntro: Change mean operating time and mean repair time. The calculator uses the lecture convention MTBF = MTTF + MTTR and a simplified long-run availability ratio.

checks.prompt: MTTF stays the same while MTTR halves. What can improve?
options: Availability, without necessarily changing failure frequency.
The number of underlying faults must halve.
The system must now have zero downtime.
feedback: Correct. Less time repairing improves the operating-time proportion.
A faster restoration procedure can leave the original fault unchanged.
A shorter repair duration is not zero downtime.

checks.prompt: A mocked unit test passes for a database adapter. What is still unproven?
options: Whether the caller handles the mocked result.
Whether the real database integration behaves as expected.
feedback: That selected caller behaviour may be exactly what the test established.
Correct. Exercise the real boundary to claim integration evidence.
A passing run already shows that this test executed.
